findings.what: Training labels are assigned before the 90-day window closes
findings.evidence: 101 of 1200 rows (8.4%) are labeled 0 with fewer than 90 days observed; those rows carry 33% more MQLs than the rest (p_BH = 0.027)
findings.action: Label = NULL, not 0, when snapshot_date + 90d > today. Re-label the 101 affected rows and add the rule to the labeling job.
findings.cost: one rule in the labeling job
findings.expect: the next model is not taught that marketing-engaged accounts fail

findings.what: Accounts are being scored on information older than the feature window
findings.evidence: 102 of 300 scoring accounts have a snapshot over 180 days old; 218 are over 90 days, and every feature is a 90-day window
findings.action: Refresh before assigning. No account over 180 days enters an arm without a refreshed snapshot.
findings.cost: enrichment refresh on ~1/3 of the batch
findings.expect: reps stop calling a description of a company from two quarters ago

findings.what: The model's own arithmetic promises more conversions than the business sees
findings.evidence: predicted probabilities sum to 19.7 conversions across 300 accounts (6.55%), against a field rate the brief puts at 1-3% (i.e. 3-9 conversions)
findings.action: Do not publish probabilities to any user or Salesforce field. Use the score only for the disagreement analysis in RECONCILE.
findings.expect: nobody forecasts off a number that is 2-6x the observed rate

findings.what: Conversations that would fill the vendor's coverage gap already happen, and are not captured
findings.evidence: 197 of 481 contacts (41%) are with accounts that have no vendor record; 67 such accounts have had at least one call. Vendor COVERAGE predicts conversion (8.22% vs 3.94%, p=0.003) but its SCORE does not (quintiles flat, p=0.42)
findings.action: Record sales calls with per-call disclosure and transcript-only storage, and extract intent per the contract in llm.py. Start with the fill_gap quadrant -- it needs no new outreach, only capture of calls that already happen.
findings.cost: recording + transcription on existing calls; no new rep time
findings.expect: the 40% of the base the vendor cannot see gets a first-hand intent signal

findings.what: The intent vendor overstates on accounts we can check
findings.evidence: of 12 accounts with both a vendor score and a call, 1 are scored high by the vendor and read low from the conversation (overall agreement 50%). ⚠ synthetic demo data — the METHOD is the deliverable, not this number
findings.action: Run this table monthly on real calls and take it into the renewal. Pay for coverage, which predicts (p=0.003); stop paying for the score, which does not (p=0.42).
findings.expect: the renewal is negotiated on evidence instead of the vendor's claim

findings.what: The model ranks accounts that declined ABOVE accounts that are ready to buy
findings.evidence: on accounts with a transcript, mean score is 6.9% for those that said no vs 5.5% for those that said yes — inverted. The cause is contact count (3.2 vs 2.0), the model's strongest feature. ⚠ synthetic demo transcripts; the mechanism is audit §3.5, which is not
findings.action: Never rank on this score. Where a conversation exists, it overrides; where it does not, use the explore arm rather than the score. Breaking the loop requires a signal that is not a function of our own past effort.
findings.cost: 0 — it is the policy this pipeline already implements
findings.expect: effort stops concentrating on accounts that are expensive because they have already been expensive

findings.what: The conversation layer changes decisions the score alone would get wrong
findings.evidence: on 20 accounts with a transcript: 2 rescued (bottom-quartile score, prospect stated budget or timeline), 5 released (24 contacts going into accounts that said no). Extraction measured at 100% on ready_to_act against known ground truth. ⚠ synthetic demo transcripts — the mechanism is the finding, not the count
findings.action: Extend recording to the 67 accounts in the fill-gap quadrant first: they already receive calls, so this needs no new rep time. Measure the same table against real outcomes at day 90.
findings.cost: recording and transcription on calls that already happen
findings.expect: the same 35% decision-change rate across the 170 accounts that have had a call, not just 20

findings.what: account_type does not mean what it says
findings.evidence: 341 of 402 training 'Suspects' and 86 of 101 scoring ones have an MQL, trial or contact; conversion is identical across the three types (chi2 p = 0.84)
findings.action: Bulk-reclassify the 86 scoring accounts, and add a validation rule so an account with activity cannot be saved as Suspect.
findings.cost: one bulk update + one validation rule
findings.expect: the VP stops seeing 'Suspects' near the top of a list and losing trust in it

findings.what: Trials with zero active users are ambiguous
findings.evidence: 19 scoring accounts started a trial and show 0 active users; in training these convert at 11.0% (8 of 73), better than trials with 1-2 users
findings.action: Ask product whether these are provisioned-but-never-used or missing seat telemetry. If telemetry, instrument it — the field is currently unreadable.
findings.cost: one question to product; instrumentation if it is the second
findings.expect: a real signal becomes readable instead of being two different things in one field

findings.what: web_touchpoints_90d cannot distinguish 'no visits' from 'not measured'
findings.evidence: 103 scoring accounts show 0; in training, 0 converts at 7.4% vs 4.5% for 1-3 (Fisher p = 0.119 — directional, not established)
findings.action: Data contract with the attribution vendor: return NULL when no measurement was taken. Until then, treat 0 as unknown rather than as a measured zero.
findings.expect: a 40%-coverage problem stops being invisible because it looks like data

findings.what: It is unknown whether sales_contacts_90d precedes the outcome window or overlaps it
findings.evidence: sales_contacts_90d is a 90-day count and the label is 'converted within 90 days'. Nothing in the files states the relationship. This is the only feature with credible signal (OR 2.2 at >=4, robust to every adjustment)
findings.action: One question to the data owner: does the contact window PRECEDE the snapshot, or is it the same 90 days in which conversion is measured? If it overlaps, the one signal in this dataset is leakage and nothing built on it is real.
findings.expect: either the exploit arm is justified, or the whole dataset is known to be unusable

findings.what: The model's ranking has never been validated out of sample in production
findings.evidence: audit §2: in-sample AUC 0.759 sits at the median of what the same architecture scores on random labels (p = 0.575); out-of-fold 0.573; forward in time 0.474, below chance
findings.action: Re-run the permutation null and the forward-chaining split (audit §2.2, §2.6a) whenever the model or the data pipeline changes. No metric gets reported without a temporal split — that is how the last one shipped.
findings.expect: the next model cannot die quietly the way this one did

findings.what: One cycle of 30 accounts per arm cannot resolve a realistic difference
findings.evidence: simulated at the brief's 1-3% field rate with NO true difference between arms, the observed spread is 3.3% and every confidence interval overlaps every other. Detecting a 50% relative lift at this base rate needs roughly 1,500 accounts per arm
findings.action: Run the arms continuously and read cumulatively, not once. Commit to the cycle for at least two quarters before drawing a conclusion, and say so up front so nobody reads cycle 1 as an answer.
findings.cost: patience, and saying this to the VP before the first readout rather than after
findings.expect: nobody kills or ships the approach on a number that cannot support either

bypassed.reason: only 20 of 170 accounts with a logged call have a transcript, and those transcripts are synthetic
bypassed.unblocked_by: recording every call; then coverage equals the fill_gap + calibrate quadrants above
bypassed.would_produce: intent for all 170 accounts with a logged call, not 20

artifacts.experiment_card:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ AGENT · experiment_card   [template]
│ purpose     : Write the week's allocation as an experiment the manager can approve or refuse
│ sensitivity : aggregate
│ routed to   : cloud
│ reads       : arms (name, size, selection rule), matching variables, base rate, readout date
│ returns     : markdown, ~150 words
├─ SYSTEM ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ You write experiment cards for an SDR manager who is not technical and
│ is sceptical of being experimented on. Be concrete about what each arm
│ is testing and what result would make us stop. Never oversell, and never
│ promise a lift number we do not have.
├─ PROMPT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ This week's allocation splits 90 accounts into 3 matched arms
│ (industry and company size). Base rate is 6.5% in training, 1-3% per the business.
│ 
│ - **exploit** (30 accounts): highest logged contact count — the rule that beats the model out-of-sample
│ - **explore** (30 accounts): never contacted but carrying a signal (trial, MQL or web activity)
│ - **control** (30 accounts): the rep picks — this is what would happen without the system
│ 
│ Write the experiment card the SDR manager reads before approving. For each arm state the
│ hypothesis in one sentence, the result that would confirm it, and the result that would
│ kill it. End with the readout date and one sentence on why the control arm exists.
├─ RETURNS (worked example) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
│ (no worked example)
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
artifacts.hygiene_suspects:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ AGENT · hygiene_batch   [template]
│ purpose     : Turn a detected CRM defect into an approval note with evidence and a preventive rule
│ sensitivity : account_ids
│ routed to   : local
│ reads       : defect, detection rule, affected count, examples, proposed correction
│ returns     : markdown, ~100 words
├─ SYSTEM ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ You write CRM correction proposals for approval in bulk. State the
│ evidence before the fix. Always include the rule that prevents the
│ defect from coming back — a one-off cleanup is worth much less than the
│ rule.
├─ PROMPT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ Defect: account_type is stale
│ Detected by: Suspect with an MQL, a trial, or a logged sales contact
│ Affected records: 86 in the scoring batch, 341 in training history
│ Examples: ACC-00160, ACC-00275, ACC-00989
│ Proposed correction: reclassify to Prospect
│ 
│ Write the approval note. Lead with the evidence, then the correction, then the preventive
│ rule. Say plainly what happens if this is not fixed.
├─ RETURNS (worked example) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
│ **account_type is stale — 86 records.** A 'Suspect' is defined as an account that fits the profile but has shown no engagement. These 86 have an MQL, a trial or a logged sales contact (e.g. ACC-00095, ACC-00228, ACC-00284), and in training this group converts at the same rate as Prospects (chi2 p = 0.84). Proposed: reclassify to Prospect in bulk. Preventive rule: a validation rule so an account with activity cannot be saved as Suspect. Left alone, the field keeps disagreeing with itself and nobody can explain why a 'Suspect' is near the top of a list.
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
artifacts.run_verdict:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ AGENT · run_verdict   [template]
│ purpose     : Say whether this week's run is worth trusting, and recommend what to do about it
│ sensitivity : aggregate
│ routed to   : cloud
│ reads       : PSI table, overlap with previous run, score concentration, flags in top K, sum of probabilities vs the field rate
│ returns     : one paragraph, under 120 words
├─ SYSTEM ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ You write a weekly one-paragraph verdict on whether a scoring run is
│ worth trusting. You are allowed — expected — to say it is not. End with
│ a concrete recommendation for THIS week, not a general observation.
├─ PROMPT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ Run of 2026-08-01. every feature is stable against training (max PSI 0.06, intent_score). Overlap of the top 30 with the previous run:
│ 30/30. the model's top-30 shares only 11/30 accounts with a plain sort by contact count. Of the top 30, 7 carry no flags. The model's predicted
│ probabilities sum to 19.7 expected conversions across 300 accounts (6.6%), against a
│ field rate the business reports at 1-3%.
│ 
│ Write the manager's paragraph. End with one concrete recommendation for this week.
├─ RETURNS (worked example) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
│ Run of 2026-08-01. Every feature is stable against training (max PSI 0.06); snapshot age is not — but that is how the batch was drawn, not drift. The top 30 shares 21 of 30 accounts with last week's list even though no underlying data changed, which is the model's own seed, not the market. Only 7 of the top 30 carry no flags at all. The model expects 19.7 conversions across 300 accounts (6.6%) against a field rate the business reports at 1–3%. Recommendation this week: run the exploit arm off sales_contacts, not off the score, and do not publish the probabilities.
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
